title: Artificial Intelligence and regulation — CILEx Regulation (CRL) position page on AI risks, opportunities and its regulatory approach
pub: CILEx Regulation Ltd (CRL) — independent regulator of CILEX members (Chartered Legal Executives, paralegals and other legal professionals), cilexregulation.org.uk
author: CILEx Regulation Ltd

dom.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: CRL directly supports the cluster’s supervised-copilot framing: AI should assist rather than displace professional judgement, with lawyers continuing to validate outputs and remain accountable. Its plans for proportionate regulation, training, assessment controls and updated guidance also align with the cluster’s emphasis on competence protection and organisational complements.
qs: In the short-term at least, it is anticipated that regulation will continue very much in the same way as at present with firms and lawyers using AI as a tool and taking responsibility for decisions being made and actions taken (validation).

We will also be looking to:  - inform the CILEX community about the use and implications of AI - consider how use of AI by students may be impacting on the education assessment process towards qualification and what appropriate control measures can be in put in place to maintain efficacy.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: CRL supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI should assist rather than replace legal judgment, with lawyers validating outputs and retaining responsibility for decisions and actions. It also endorses proportionate regulation, updated guidance and training, but does not materially assess whether verification burdens consume efficiency gains or address lifecycle confidentiality controls in detail.
qs: In the short-term at least, it is anticipated that regulation will continue very much in the same way as at present with firms and lawyers using AI as a tool and taking responsibility for decisions being made and actions taken (validation).
The level of regulation needs to be proportionate, and enable the use of the new technology.

kp.k: AI presents legal opportunities alongside material risks
kp.d: CRL frames AI adoption as an evolving professional challenge: legal professionals should seek efficiency and other benefits while actively mitigating associated risks. This is a regulatory position rather than an empirical finding.
qs: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology into the legal profession presents both opportunities as well as risks.
Legal professionals must be ready to navigate this evolving landscape in order to harness AI's benefits while mitigating associated risks.

kp.k: AI could improve access to justice
kp.d: CRL predicts that AI has broad potential to improve access to legal advice, court and justice-system processes, and access to justice for consumers. The page provides no study, measured outcome or implementation timeframe supporting this claim.
qs: AI has limitless potential to improve access to legal advice, streamline the justice and court system and access to justice for consumers.

kp.k: AI supports automation, analysis and legal research
kp.d: The page identifies task automation, contract analysis, legal research and data mining for case preparation as principal opportunities. It asserts that these applications can increase efficiency, strengthen cases and assist decision-making, but supplies no quantitative evidence.
qs: Enhanced efficiency – task automation, contract analysis and legal research.
Research and case preparation – efficient data mining helps build stronger cases and helps the decision making process

kp.k: Cost reductions may benefit small businesses
kp.d: CRL claims that lower operational costs from AI can create expansion opportunities for small businesses. It does not specify whether these businesses are legal providers or clients, quantify expected savings, or discuss effects on legal pricing.
qs: Cost reduction – reduced operational costs offers expansion opportunities for small businesses.

kp.k: Some legal support roles could be displaced
kp.d: CRL presents displacement of some support roles as a potential risk rather than a measured labour-market finding. It recommends adaptation by lawyers as a condition for remaining competitive, without identifying affected occupations, scale or timing.
qs: Support role implications – some support roles could be displaced. Lawyers need to adapt to remain competitive.

kp.k: Verification and human judgement remain essential
kp.d: The page identifies verification, transparency and accountability as ethical requirements and argues that AI assistance must remain balanced with human judgement. In its regulatory discussion, it calls the checking process “validation” and places responsibility on firms and lawyers for resulting decisions and actions.
qs: Ethical issues – the importance of data verification, transparency and accountability. Balancing human judgement with AI assistance is essential.

In the short-term at least, it is anticipated that regulation will continue very much in the same way as at present with firms and lawyers using AI as a tool and taking responsibility for decisions being made and actions taken (validation).

kp.k: Lawyers remain regulated decision-makers in the short term
kp.d: CRL anticipates, at least in the short term, a copilot-style model in which AI is treated as a tool and the lawyer remains the accountable decision-maker. Responsibility may attach to the individual lawyer, the firm, or both; the statement is a regulatory expectation, not evidence of current universal practice.
qs: The lawyer will remain the person making the decisions and subject to regulation, either individually and/or as part of a firm.

kp.k: AI regulation should be coordinated and proportionate
kp.d: CRL proposes collaboration with regulators inside and outside the legal sector to coordinate the response to AI. It also argues that regulation should be proportionate and should permit beneficial technological use rather than unnecessarily obstructing it.
qs: We will be looking to collaborate with other regulators within and outside of the sector to coordinate a joint regulatory response to AI.
The level of regulation needs to be proportionate, and enable the use of the new technology.

kp.k: Professional standards and training require review
kp.d: CRL plans to inform the CILEX community, review standards, codes and guidance governing AI, and consider employee training needs in regulated firms and within CRL itself. These are intended regulatory actions rather than completed reforms.
qs: inform the CILEX community about the use and implications of AI
review our standards, codes and guidance governing the use and application of AI. Consideration of training needs for employees both within firms and at CRL.

kp.k: Student AI use may undermine assessment efficacy
kp.d: CRL identifies professional formation as a regulatory concern, specifically whether students' AI use affects qualification assessments. It proposes considering controls to preserve assessment efficacy but does not report evidence of misconduct or specify particular measures.
qs: consider how use of AI by students may be impacting on the education assessment process towards qualification and what appropriate control measures can be in put in place to maintain efficacy.

kp.k: CRL may use AI in its operations
kp.d: The regulator intends to examine whether AI can improve the effectiveness and efficiency of its own regulatory and business operations. The page describes an area for consideration, not a deployed system or demonstrated result.
qs: consider how AI can be used effectively by CRL to improving the effectiveness and efficiency of our own regulation and business operation.

kp.k: Ethical and societal implications constrain AI adoption
kp.d: CRL concludes that efficiency and innovation opportunities must be considered alongside ethical, professional and societal implications. This qualification reinforces its position that adoption should occur under continuing human responsibility and regulatory oversight.
qs: While AI presents opportunities for efficiency and innovation, careful consideration of ethical, professional, and societal implications is essential.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: CRL identifies potential improvements in access to justice, efficiency, case preparation and costs, alongside possible support-role displacement and continuing human responsibility.
pts.d: CRL claims that AI can improve access to legal advice and justice and streamline courts and the justice system. It identifies automation, contract analysis and legal research as efficiency opportunities, and suggests efficient data mining can strengthen cases and assist decision-making. Reduced operational costs are presented as an opportunity for small businesses to expand. CRL warns that some support roles could be displaced and that lawyers must adapt to remain competitive. Its anticipated short-term regulatory approach is augmentation rather than autonomous substitution: lawyers use AI as a tool while remaining responsible for decisions and actions. CRL also proposes considering AI's effects on qualification assessments, reviewing standards and training needs, and exploring AI to improve its own regulatory and business operations; these are intentions rather than reported outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are CRL's qualitative regulatory assessment, without supporting empirical results in the supplied page.
pts.d: The page supplies no quantitative data, benchmarks, case studies or measured outcomes for its claims about access, efficiency, costs or displacement. It links to a July 2024 webinar, describes a product demonstration, and lists additional resources, but does not reproduce findings from them. The demonstration is not presented as proof of the claimed benefits, and CRL expressly disclaims affiliation or endorsement. Statements about the regulatory approach are CRL's own expectations and intentions as a regulator.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Regulatory continuity is explicitly a short-term expectation; other benefits, risks and planned actions have no fixed timetable.
pts.d: In this 2024 position page, CRL describes generative AI tools as already available and gaining prominence. Access, efficiency and cost benefits are framed as opportunities or potential, and displacement as a possibility, without adoption forecasts or deadlines. CRL qualifies its expectation of largely unchanged regulation with 'In the short-term at least'. Responsible use requires human judgement, data verification, transparency and accountability, with lawyers retaining responsibility. Regulation should be proportionate and enable technology use. Collaboration, standards reviews, assessment controls, training consideration and internal AI exploration are prospective activities without specified completion dates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include consumers, courts, lawyers and firms, support staff, small businesses, qualification students and CRL itself.
pts.d: Consumers could gain improved access to advice and justice, while courts and the justice system could become more streamlined. Lawyers and firms could improve research, case preparation and efficiency but retain responsibility for AI-assisted work and face adaptation and training needs. Support workers face possible displacement, although the page does not identify particular roles or quantify exposure. Small businesses are identified as potential beneficiaries of reduced operational costs and expansion opportunities. Students' AI use may affect qualification assessments, prompting consideration of controls. The CILEX community is an intended audience for information about AI, while CRL and its employees are affected through training, regulatory review, cross-regulator coordination and potential internal operational improvements.
